chapter: The Famous Door, Billy May and the Palomar fire
title: The Ellingtonized band, the New Penn Club and the power of live radio
summary: Around 1937 his band took a job at the New Penn Club outside Pittsburgh for its broadcast wire; he explains live radio mattered more than records then.

story.theme_name: Radio and television work: staff jobs, shows and broadcasts
story.community_name: Working radio and television: network shows, studio staffs, talk-show bands

blocks.x: We were along about '37, before we got into your movies, and you'd been to the Glenn Island Casino and you were in New York. You talked about Duke at the Cotton Club and Andy Gibson writing for your band, right?

That's right. I had this band that I was rehearsing which was Ellingtonized. In other words it was in the direction of the Ellington approach to music. And of course we still had a lot of problems getting decent jobs. And we went out to the New Penn Club, right outside of Pittsburgh, which also had a broadcast wire, a national broadcast wire, because that was the big thing in those days.

You had to get on the air, and records really weren't that important, which is strange. I mean they were important in a sense, but as compared to today, it was like night and day. The live broadcasts were the things that brought people in.
At that point were records licensed for radio broadcast? They weren't were they? You had to --

Well, this is the thing that Fred Waring fought for years and got nowhere. But the fact remains that a record is a form of publication. For example, you can get in ASCAP if you've got a record of a tune, whether you have anything printed or not. You say here's the record. They recognize that as a form of publication. And therefore, if you own the -- if you bought the record you can do anything you want with it. Now, Fred was trying to say that everybody should get paid when they played the record on the radio. Well, there weren't all these disc jockeys, then. There were a few big ones like Martin Block and Al Jarvis out on the coast, and -- but nothing like today. The whole thing was live broadcasts. You've heard Steve Allen do his wonderful, "And now from atop the So-and-So Roof in Downtown Minneapolis," well, this was the way it was. From all over the country you got live broadcasts. Every night from, oh, 10:30, 11:00 o'clock on, even earlier. And there just -- there wasn't any substitute. Records alone wouldn't do it in those days.
Well, didn't it work in a way that if
you were heard on the radio a lot then there became a demand for you and then you got bookings?
